卡龍琴名稱源自古代希臘語「規則、法律、規範、原則」。其起源之一可追溯至舊亞述帝國: The name qanun comes from the ancient Greek for 'rule, law, standard, principle'. One account of its origin traces it to the Old Assyrian period, in nineteenth-century BCE Mesopotamia, carved on an ivory box excavated at Nimrud. It is current in Armenia, Iran, modern Turkey, Greece, the Arab East and the Maghreb of North Africa, and was later carried by Arab migrants to West Africa and Central Asia. Turkish musicologists record that the small mandal tuning levers appeared about thirty years before 1922; after electronic tuners became widespread, tuning positions became increasingly standardised. Armenia uses equal semitones, the Arab world quarter tones and Turkey 72 equal divisions, and this is an important variable in playing the modes and in modulating.
卡龍琴為大型齊特琴，薄梯形共鳴板承弦，弦振經長橋傳入板面，音色常被描述為具戲劇性: The qanun is a large zither whose thin trapezoidal soundboard carries the strings; the vibration of the strings passes through a long bridge into the board, and the timbre is often described as dramatic. The Arab form usually supports a single long bridge on five leather patches and the Turkish on four, which gives the Arab form more room to fit very low and very high strings. The decorative soundholes (kafes) affect the customary timbre, and their position varies by region. The standard range is about three and a half octaves, from A2 to E6, and the Arab form can extend to F2 and G6. It is plucked with a tortoiseshell plectrum or the fingernails; the tuning levers (mandal) allow the pitch to be adjusted while playing, and the source does not say how the volume is controlled.
卡龍琴為弦鳴樂器，演奏時置於膝上，採坐姿或蹲姿，亦可放在支架上。發聲靠雙手持玳瑁: The qanun is a chordophone, held on the lap when played, either seated or squatting, or set on a stand. It sounds when the player plucks with a tortoiseshell plectrum in each hand or with the fingernails; under each course is a small mandal lever that can be raised or lowered quickly during playing, changing the speaking length and so fine-tuning the pitch. A beginner should first get used to the standard range of about three and a half octaves and to the plucking positions, then check the mandal layout against a tuner, and practise working the levers while plucking.

The player plucks with two tortoiseshell plectra or with the fingernails. Under each course is a small metal lever or catch (mandal).
